Half of Nearby Galaxies Hide an Active Black Hole

Author

TidyTuesday | 2026-08-11

Published

August 11, 2026

Introduction

Point a spectrograph at the centre of a nearby galaxy and — around half the time — you will find a supermassive black hole actively swallowing matter. That was the surprise of the Palomar Spectroscopic Survey of Nearby Galaxies: in the 1990s, astronomers used the 200-inch Hale Telescope — then the world’s largest — to split the light of 486 galaxy nuclei into spectra and classify what powered each one (Ho, Filippenko & Sargent 1995, 1997, 2009).

This report explores the collected data with three questions, all of which turn into clear, standalone visuals.

The Three Questions

  1. Can two emission-line ratios separate star-forming galaxies from black holes? The famous BPT diagram (Baldwin, Phillips & Terlevich 1981);
  2. Does a galaxy’s shape predict what happens at its centre? — morphology vs. nuclear activity along the Hubble sequence;
  3. Do more massive galaxies host more active nuclei? — stellar velocity dispersion (a black-hole-mass proxy) vs. activity type.

Data & Methodology

  • Source: Palomar Spectroscopic Survey, via VizieR (Ho, Filippenko & Sargent 1995, 1997, 2009).
  • Probe: optical emission-line spectra of 486 galaxy nuclei taken with the Hale Telescope.
  • Classification: each nucleus is typed as H II (star formation), Seyfert (luminous AGN), LINER (low-ionisation AGN), Transition (composite), or Absorption. 415 nuclei are classified; 71 lack detectable emission lines.
  • BPT ratios: the dataset’s log_* columns are linear intensity ratios, not logarithms — log10() is applied here to build the diagram (see analysis.R).
Activity Galaxies Share of classified
H II 203 48.9%
LINER 94 22.7%
Transition 65 15.7%
Seyfert 52 12.5%
Absorption 1 0.2%

Data quality note. About 15% of survey galaxies have no emission lines and cannot be classified. Roughly one in five classifications is flagged uncertain or very uncertain — these are drawn faded in Figure 1. No physical claims beyond the reported classifications: this is a demographics snapshot of the local universe.

Finding 1 — Two line ratios split star formation from black holes

Alt text: BPT diagnostic diagram, 406 nuclei, log[NII]/H-alpha on the x-axis and log[OIII]/H-beta on the y-axis. Points coloured by activity type: blue H II galaxies form a cloud at lower left; red Seyferts a spur at upper right; orange LINERs scatter to the right; green transitions sit between. Two dashed boundary curves cut the plane; uncertain galaxies are paler.

The diagram works like a referee: it separates photoionisation by young stars (H II regions) from photoionisation by a black hole’s accretion disk (AGN). The ionising power axis (y) is what does the heavy lifting:

  • Seyfert nuclei cluster at the top — median 0.75 in log[OIII]/Hβ, the signature of hard, energetic radiation;
  • H II galaxies sit at the bottom-left at -0.31 — soft, stellar radiation;
  • LINERs occupy the right-hand side: enough gas to glow, but too little ionising power to be a classic active nucleus.

The dashed boundaries (Kauffmann 2003 / Kewley 2001) are theoretical limits: nearly all star-forming galaxies fall below the blue line, and above the purple line star formation is no longer a plausible engine.

Finding 2 — Shape predicts destiny

Alt text: 100% stacked horizontal bars along the Hubble sequence (Elliptical, Lenticular, Spiral, Barred spiral, Irregular). Segments coloured by activity type, with per-cell galaxy counts labelled. Early-type galaxies are dominated by orange LINER segments; late types by blue H II.

Morphology Dominant nucleus Share
Elliptical LINER (AGN) 73%
Lenticular (S0) LINER / Transition 42% / 34%
Spiral H II (star-forming) 59%
Barred spiral H II 55%
Irregular H II 100%

Scrolling along the Hubble sequence, the galaxy’s soul changes: early-type, gas-poor systems (E, S0) host quiet, low-luminosity AGN (LINERs), while late-type, gas-rich systems (spirals, irregulars) are full of young stars. This is a demographics result of the local universe — most galaxies are either “asleep giants” or “star factories”, with relatively few in between.

Finding 3 — Bigger galaxies, busier black holes

Alt text: vertical violin plots of stellar velocity dispersion (log scale) by activity type, ordered H II, Transition, Seyfert, LINER. Filled by activity colour with jittered points; white dots mark medians (70, 135, 149, 167 km/s). Dispersion rises from H II to LINER.

The M-sigma relation ties a galaxy’s central black-hole mass to its stellar velocity dispersion: measure σ and you have a handle on the black hole. Splitting the sample by activity reveals a clean ladder:

  • H II (star-forming) nuclei live in the lightest galaxies — median 69.8 km/s;
  • LINER nuclei, in the heaviest — median 167 km/s;
  • Seyferts and transitions sit between (148.75 and 135.3 km/s).

More massive galaxy → more massive black hole → a more energetic (or at least more recognisable) active nucleus. Exactly the demographics the Palomar team reported by eye in 1997, now visible in one panel.

The Big Picture

Put the three figures back together: black holes are not rare. Around 51% of nearby galaxies show some AGN signature (Seyfert, LINER, or transition) against 49% pure star formation. The engine sits in the galaxy’s centre, and how we see it depends on how massive the system is and how much gas is left to feed it.

Reproducibility

  • analysis.R — full pipeline: cleaning, morphology binning, and all three figures.
  • outputs/ — key_numbers.csv (all headline statistics) and hubble_strip.csv.
  • figures/*.png — the three charts above.
  • Data: palomar_survey.csv, palomar_emission_lines.csv (TidyTuesday 2026-08-11, via VizieR).
